query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy coatings, wear resistance is controlled by a strain‐induced phase transformation at the sliding interface that forms a robust tribolayer. Tailored addition of a specific element (e.g., Ti or a similar element with a large atomic radius) is predicted to shift the transformation threshold, thereby modulating the formation and effectiveness of the tribolayer and consequently improving wear performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating (e.g., baseline composition similar to AlCrFeNiV) that initially exhibits a mixed microstructure with no deliberately tuned phase transformation threshold.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition through targeted element addition designed to trigger (or suppress) the strain-induced phase transformation during wear (using, for example, incremental additions of Ti), while maintaining identical processing and testing conditions.
generation.conditions: Identical, controlled wear testing conditions (e.g., constant load, sliding speed, ambient temperature) using pin‐on‐disk experiments combined with in situ microscopy (SEM) and local thermal/hardness measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a strain-induced transformed phase at the wear interface that develops into a robust, protective tribolayer.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding wear, high localized stresses induce a phase transformation at the surface; the resulting transformed phase rearranges into a dense tribolayer that resists abrasive and delamination wear. Adjusting the alloy composition alters the stress threshold required to trigger this phase transformation, thereby directly affecting the tribolayer’s formation and, consequently, the coating’s wear performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline composition, the modified alloy with targeted element addition is expected to exhibit a measurable decrease in wear rate and improved frictional behavior due to earlier or more extensive formation of the protective tribolayer. The effect should be observable consistently under the standardized wear testing conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline high-entropy alloy coating without the tailored element addition that does not exhibit the adjusted transformation threshold, resulting in a less effective tribolayer formation and higher wear rate.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold under moderate to high sliding stresses at ambient temperature, within the compositional window of high-entropy alloys designed for wear-resistance. It may not directly apply if external factors (e.g., severe oxidation, extreme temperatures, or large-scale compositional segregation) dominate the wear mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds for the phase transformation and the exact magnitude of wear reduction are uncertain and may vary with the specific element addition and processing conditions. Additionally, competing mechanisms such as oxidation could influence the observed wear behavior, requiring careful isolation of the phase transformation effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings under identical processing conditions. One set is the baseline (no targeted element addition) and the other set includes incremental additions of a chosen element (e.g., Ti). Perform pin‐on‐disk wear tests under constant load, sliding speed, and temperature. Use in situ SEM imaging with local thermal and hardness measurements to monitor phase transformation and tribolayer formation at the wear interface.
measurements: Characterization of surface phases (XRD, SEM, TEM) to detect the presence and extent of the transformed phase
In situ local hardness and thermal measurements during wear
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the targeted element addition does not lead to an earlier onset or a greater extent of the strain-induced phase transformation at the wear interface, and if no statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower wear rate and improved friction behavior) is observed compared to the baseline coating, then the hypothesis that this strain-induced phase transformation governs wear performance is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with high hardness are promising materials for advanced industrial manufacturing. In this study, the AlCrFeNiV HEA was designed and successfully prepared using a plasma instantaneous process. The hardness test showed that AlCrFeNiV had a high hardness of 1076 ± 15 HV, which was much higher than those reported in the literature. The microstructure of AlCrFeNiV was composed of two different types of body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, BCC1 (Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni) and BCC2 (enriched V and Cr). A mixture of different BCC systems produced solution strengthening, which was responsible for the superior hardness. Moreover, the reciprocating sliding wear behavior of HEA against Al2O3 balls under dry and lubricated conditions at ambient temperature was investigated. The wear rates of AlCrFeNiV against Al2O3 under dry wear and lubrication were 17.2 × 10−5 mm3 N−1·m−1 and 12.4 × 10−5 mm3N−1·m−1, respectively, which were of the same order of magnitude as the wear rates of BCC HEAs. Regardless of the dry wear or wear with lubrication, the wear mechanism of the HEA was abrasive and delamination wear.

In contrast, the BCC phase has a looser structure than the FCC phase. chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by proposing a testable mechanistic hypothesis: that wear performance is governed by a strain-induced phase transformation that forms a robust tribolayer. The experiment controls the alloy composition (the lever) to manipulate this mechanism. The approach fills the gap by extending previous work—which may have observed correlations without a controlled study—into a rigorous controlled-variable experiment using standard wear testing techniques in materials science.
